Sum
sum
n. (a total, the whole of a reckoning; also the substance or gist of a matter; rendering Hebrew rosh, Greek kephalaion)
From Latin summa, the top, the highest — because Roman accountants added upward and wrote the total at the head of the column. Both Hebrew rosh and Greek kephalaion likewise mean head, so all three languages call a total the head of the reckoning.

Biblical Definition

A sum is a total, and the word carries both an arithmetical and a rhetorical sense in Scripture. Arithmetically, taking the sum of Israel is the census, and it comes with an unexpected requirement: “When thou takest the sum of the children of Israel after their number, then shall they give every man a ransom for his soul unto the LORD” (Exodus 30:12) — counting the people is dangerous, because a census is a reckoning of a strength that is not the king's, and David learned the danger the hard way. The half-shekel ransom acknowledges that every counted man is a redeemed man. Luke gives a memorable commercial use: the chief captain, hearing Paul claim Roman citizenship, says “With a great sum obtained I this freedom” — and Paul answers, “But I was free born” (Acts 22:28), an exchange in which purchased status meets birthright, and which every Christian may read twice over. The psalmist uses the word for something uncountable: “How precious also are thy thoughts unto me, O God! how great is the sum of them!” (Psalm 139:17). And Hebrews uses the rhetorical sense to head its central argument: “Now of the things which we have spoken this is the sum: We have such an high priest, who is set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens” (Hebrews 8:1) — the whole epistle reduced to one clause.

Webster 1828 Definition

A total, and the substance of a matter. The census sum requires a ransom for every counted man; a Roman captain bought his citizenship with a great sum where Paul was free born; and Hebrews heads its central argument with this is the sum.

expand to see more

SUM, n. [L. summa, from summus, highest.] The aggregate of two or more numbers, magnitudes, quantities or particulars; the amount or whole of any number of individuals or particulars added.

2. A quantity of money or currency; any amount indefinitely.

3. Compendium; abridgment; the amount; the substance.

4. Height; completion.

SUM, v.t. To add particulars into one whole; to collect two or more particular numbers into one number.

Key Scripture

Exodus 30:12 — "When thou takest the sum of the children of Israel after their number, then shall they give every man a ransom for his soul unto the LORD, when thou numberest them; that there be no plague among them, when thou numberest them."

Acts 22:28 — "And the chief captain answered, With a great sum obtained I this freedom. And Paul said, But I was free born."

Psalm 139:17 — "How precious also are thy thoughts unto me, O God! how great is the sum of them!"

Hebrews 8:1 — "Now of the things which we have spoken this is the sum: We have such an high priest, who is set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens;"

Modern Corruption

The instinct to measure a work of God by its totals — attendance, giving, converts counted — repeats the sin of David's census, in which numbering a strength that belongs to God became an act of self-congratulation.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself; the corruption is a practice rather than a lexical shift. Exodus 30:12 attaches a ransom to every census, and 2 Samuel 24 records what happens when a king numbers his people without one: David's heart smote him afterward, and Joab — not a tender man — had tried to talk him out of it. The problem is not arithmetic. Scripture counts constantly; the fourth book of the Bible is named for a census. The problem is a reckoning undertaken to measure one's own strength, which turns God's gift into an inventory of assets. The modern equivalent is not hard to identify: the ministry report in which numbers do the work that faithfulness should, the pastor who knows his attendance to the person and his congregation's sins not at all, the denominational statistic that decides which churches are serious. Counting is lawful; counting in order to be impressed is the census sin.

The principle to recover is the one Hebrews 8:1 models. When the writer says this is the sum, he is not totalling results but stating substance: we have such an high priest. That is the reckoning by which a church should be measured — what it has in Christ and what it holds of the truth — and it does not vary with the attendance. Psalm 139 supplies the counterweight from the other side: God's thoughts toward His people are more in number than the sand, a sum no one is asked to total. The man who is content to be numbered among a people he cannot count, by a God whose thoughts toward him he cannot count either, has escaped the temptation entirely.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rosh (head, and so a total — lift up the head is the idiom for taking a census); Greek kephalaion (the chief point, sum) from kephale, head; Latin summa, the top.

expand to see more

Hebrew rosh (H7218) — head, top, sum; in the idiom nasa rosh, to lift the head, meaning to take a census.

Hebrew miphqad (H4662) — a mustering, numbering; the term for the census in 2 Samuel 24:9.

Greek kephalaion (G2774) — the chief point, main thing, sum; the word in Hebrews 8:1 and Acts 22:28.

Greek kephale (G2776) — head; the root, which is why a total is called a sum in three languages.

Hebrew kopher (H3724) — a ransom, covering price; the half-shekel required of every man counted in Exodus 30:12.

Usage

"“When thou takest the sum… then shall they give every man a ransom” — every counted man is a redeemed man."

"“With a great sum obtained I this freedom… But I was free born” — purchased status meets birthright."

"“This is the sum: We have such an high priest” — a whole epistle reduced to one clause."
